title: At the restaurant
goal: Read a Turkish menu, order food, and say what you want to do with the pattern *-mek istemek*.
bekal: build "I want to ..." sentences from any verb
order, ask for the check, and ask what's in a dish
recognize the dish names you'll meet on every menu

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Akşam yemeği
dialogs.intro: Emre takes Budi to a small restaurant in Kadıköy. The waiter comes over with the menu.

lines.speaker: Garson:
lines.text: Bugün mercimek çorbası ve İskender çok iyi.
lines.id: Today the lentil soup and the İskender are very good.
lines.literal: today lentil soup-its and Iskender very good.

lines.speaker: Emre:
lines.text: Döner, pide, domates sosu ve yoğurt. Çok lezzetli.
lines.id: Döner, pide bread, tomato sauce and yogurt. It's delicious.
lines.literal: döner, pide, tomato sauce-its and yogurt. very tasty.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tamam, onu denemek istiyorum. Ama önce bir soru: eti helal mi?
lines.id: OK, I want to try that. But first, one question: is the meat halal?
lines.literal: OK, that-the to-try am-wanting-I. but first a question: meat-its halal question?

lines.speaker: Garson:
lines.text: Tabii, bütün etlerimiz helal. Domuz eti yok.
lines.id: Of course, all our meat is halal. There's no pork.
lines.literal: of-course, all meat-s-our halal. pig meat-its there-isn't.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Güzel. Bir İskender ve bir ayran lütfen.
lines.id: Great. One İskender and one ayran, please.
lines.literal: nice. one Iskender and one ayran please.

lines.speaker: Emre:
lines.text: Bana da bir Adana kebap. Acılı olsun.
lines.id: And an Adana kebab for me. Make it spicy.
lines.literal: me-to too one Adana kebab. spicy let-it-be.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Evet, bir mercimek çorbası içmek istiyorum.
lines.id: Yes, I'd like a lentil soup.
lines.literal: yes, one lentil soup-its to-drink am-wanting-I.

lines.speaker: Garson:
lines.id: Coming right up. Enjoy your meal!

notes: **Soup is drunk, not eaten.** Turkish uses *içmek* for soup — and for cigarettes too (*sigara içmek*). Whatever goes down without chewing is drunk.

**Afiyet olsun is said before OR after eating**, by anyone to anyone who's eating. The reply is *teşekkürler*. To the cook, say *elinize sağlık* — "health to your hands", the highest compliment for food in Turkey.

**Acılı means "with chili", acısız "without chili".** These two endings — *-lı* (with) and *-sız* (without) — are taken apart in Unit 18, but they show up on menus first: *şekerli* (with sugar), *şekersiz*, *sütlü* (with milk), *tuzsuz* (unsalted).

**Olsun means "let it be".** In the dialogue, *acılı olsun* = "let it be spicy". The word appears in many wishes and set phrases: *afiyet olsun*, *geçmiş olsun* (get well soon), *kolay gelsin* (may it come easy), *başınız sağ olsun* (my condolences).

sections.title: I want to — the pattern -mek istemek

blocks.text: To say "I want to do something", Turkish uses the **full dictionary form** (ending in *-mek/-mak*) followed by *istemek*, which takes the person ending. The first verb doesn't change at all.
The object still stands in front of the first verb: *Bir çay içmek istiyorum* — "one tea to-drink want-I". Everything else piles up in front; only *istemek* carries the person ending.

blocks.title: İstemek can also stand alone
items: With a noun, *istemek* simply means "to want": *Su istiyorum* (I want water), *Poşet istemiyorum* (I don't want a bag).

When ordering, the short form is actually more common than a full sentence: *Bir çay lütfen* sounds far more natural than *Bir çay içmek istiyorum*. The long version is for explaining what you'd like, not for ordering.

blocks.text: A Turkish menu is built almost entirely from the two-noun pattern you learned in Unit 4: **ingredient + dish-its**. Once you see the pattern, you can guess what's on the plate without a dictionary.

blocks.title: Halal, pork, alcohol
items: Beef, chicken and lamb in Turkish restaurants are generally slaughtered according to Islamic rules, and *domuz eti* (pork) is practically never on an ordinary menu — you'll only find it in a few specialty shops in big cities.

If you keep halal, the two things worth asking about are *gelatin* in desserts, and alcohol. A restaurant labeled *içkili* serves alcoholic drinks; one labeled *içkisiz* doesn't. A useful sentence: *Bunun içinde alkol var mı?* — "Is there alcohol in this?"

blocks.title: Unit 8 review
items: Cover the Turkish and rebuild it from memory: "Where are you going?" · "I'm going to school." · "We're coming from home." · "We're taking the tram." · "Is it far from here?"
Then add the direction and origin endings to: *ev*, *okul*, *Ankara*, *iş*.
